meta.title: E-commerce Checkout
meta.summary: Place an order, reserve stock and charge the card exactly once, with a saga to undo work when payment fails.

functional: Place an order from a cart
nonFunctional: Never sell more units than are in stock
Survive payment provider timeouts and outages

scale.label: Orders
scale.value: ~20M a day (~230/s average), 5k/s at flash-sale peak

scale.label: Reads
scale.value: ~5 per order (cart, stock, order status), ~25k/s at peak

slos.name: Checkout availability
slos.sli: Order requests that succeed divided by all order requests, at the API gateway, excluding card declines

slos.name: Checkout speed
slos.sli: Order requests answered (201, 202 or 402) within the threshold, divided by all order requests, at the API gateway

slos.name: Charged exactly once
slos.sli: Paid orders with exactly one successful provider charge, divided by paid orders, from reconciliation against the provider's charge list

slos.name: Never oversold
slos.sli: SKUs whose committed reservations stay within the stock received, divided by all SKUs sold, from an audit query every 5 minutes

alerts.when: Reconciliation finds any order with more than one successful charge at the provider
alerts.why: It is money, and it breaks trust. Stop and fix.

alerts.when: Checkout errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
Checkout errors burning the error budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: A slow leak that would use up the month's budget in ten days.

alerts.when: Slow checkouts burning the latency budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Shoppers abandon slow checkouts and retry, adding load.

alerts.when: The audit finds any SKU with more committed units than stock received
alerts.why: Somebody paid for an item we do not have. Stop sales of that SKU and find the code path.

alerts.when: Payment provider timeouts and 5xx above 5% of charges for 5 minutes
alerts.why: Customers cannot pay. Open the circuit breaker so new checkouts fail fast; orders already charging stay PENDING for the sweeper.

alerts.when: Oldest unpublished outbox row above 60 seconds
alerts.why: Emails and analytics are delayed. The orders themselves are fine.
The sweeper is not settling them: the provider is still unreachable, or the sweeper itself is failing. Their stock stays held meanwhile.

alerts.when: Lock waits above 100 ms on a single SKU row
alerts.why: A flash sale concentrates writes on one row. Split the stock into buckets.

alerts.when: Email worker consumer lag above 5 minutes, or any event in the dead-letter topic
alerts.why: Confirmations are late or lost. The orders themselves are fine.

alerts.when: Orders DB CPU above 80% or connections above 85% of the maximum for 15 minutes
alerts.why: At 5k orders/s the primary is the first shared limit; slow commits show up as checkout latency.

signals.name: Outbox lag
signals.why: The age of the oldest committed event that has not been published.

signals.name: Timeouts and unknown outcomes
signals.why: A timeout leaves the charge state unknown, so track it separately from declines.

signals.name: Row lock wait time
signals.why: Contention on a hot SKU is the first thing to give in a flash sale.

signals.name: Orders by outcome
signals.why: The business view: a fall in paid orders with no rise in errors points at the provider or a front-end bug.

signals.name: Reservations held, committed and released
signals.why: Held stock that is neither committed nor released means the sweeper is behind and items look sold out.

signals.name: Blocked requests by rule
signals.why: A jump in the card-testing rate rule is an attack in progress; a jump in a managed rule after a release can be false positives.

steps: Follow the order id in the trace: did it stall at the reservation, the charge or the final commit?
Check provider timeouts and unknown outcomes, and whether the circuit breaker is open.
Check the sweeper ran in the last few minutes and what it settled.
Confirm reservations of abandoned checkouts are being released, and none of an order whose charge started.

debug.symptom: Customers were charged but got no confirmation
steps: Check outbox lag: the event may simply be late.
Check email worker errors and the provider status.
Confirm the order shows PAID in the orders database.

nodes.label: WAF
nodes.description: Web ACL on the CDN: managed rules, bot control, rate rules against card testing

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Points the shop hostname at the CDN

nodes.label: API Gateway
nodes.description: Auth, per-user rate limits, routing; reaches the services through a private integration

nodes.label: Internal Load Balancer
nodes.description: Private L7 load balancer in front of the Order Service fleet; health checks across 3 zones

nodes.label: Order Service
nodes.description: Orchestrates the checkout saga; its background sweeper settles stuck orders and releases abandoned reservations

nodes.label: Payment Service
nodes.description: Wraps the payment provider; the only holder of the provider API key; owns idempotency keys

nodes.label: Orders DB
nodes.description: orders + outbox tables in one database

nodes.label: Inventory DB
nodes.description: stock(sku, available, reserved) with CHECK (available >= 0); reservations(order_id, sku, status, expires_at)

nodes.label: Order Events
nodes.description: Kafka topic: OrderPaid, OrderFailed; a dead-letter topic for events a consumer keeps failing on

nodes.label: Outbox Relay
nodes.description: Publishes committed outbox rows to the event stream

flows.title: Place order
flows.summary: Idempotent order creation, atomic stock reservation, an idempotent charge, and a transactional outbox for the follow-up events.

steps.label: resolve shop.example.com
steps.detail: The shop hostname points at the CDN, which terminates TLS near the shopper. Resolvers cache the answer.

steps.label: POST /orders
steps.detail: The client creates an idempotency key once per checkout attempt and reuses it on retries. Only a card token from the provider (pm_visa) is sent; card numbers never reach our servers.

steps.label: managed rules, bot + rate rules
steps.detail: AWS WAF runs on the CDN edge before anything is forwarded: managed rule sets block common exploits, bot control challenges scripted clients, and rate rules on POST /orders per IP and per account stop card testing (bots trying many stolen cards with small orders).

steps.label: allowed: forward
steps.detail: Only requests the web ACL allows reach the CDN.

steps.label: forward, not cached
steps.detail: /orders has caching disabled: the CDN terminates TLS near the shopper and forwards the body, the Authorization header and the idempotency key to the origin. Responses carry Cache-Control: no-store, so one shopper's order can never be served to another.

steps.label: auth + rate limit
steps.detail: Validates the shopper's token and applies per-user limits. During a flash sale a virtual waiting room in front of checkout (not shown) can hold excess shoppers.

steps.label: create order (VPC Link)
steps.detail: The gateway reaches the private load balancer through a VPC Link, so no service is exposed to the internet. It starts a trace here; the traceparent header travels with every hop and into the outbox event.
steps.payload:
POST /internal/orders HTTP/1.1
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
X-Customer-Id: cus_19
Idempotency-Key: 9b2e4c1a-…

steps.label: to a healthy instance
steps.detail: The internal load balancer spreads requests over the Order Service instances in all three zones and stops sending to any that fail health checks. A managed gateway scales itself; the fleet behind it still needs this.

steps.label: INSERT order PENDING
steps.detail: A unique constraint on (customer, idempotency key): on a conflict the insert returns no row, so the service reads the existing order and returns its current state (201 if paid, 202 while still in progress) instead of creating a second one. A reused key with a different cart is rejected with 422.

steps.label: reserve: conditional UPDATE
steps.detail: One short transaction: the decrement only succeeds while stock remains, so two buyers can never both get the last pair, and CHECK (available >= 0) backs it up. The reservation row is unique per order and SKU, so a retried reserve changes nothing. No distributed lock needed.
steps.payload:
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO reservations (order_id, sku, qty, status, expires_at)
VALUES ('o_501', 'SHOE-42', 1, 'HELD', now() + interval '15 minutes')
ON CONFLICT (order_id, sku) DO NOTHING;  -- 0 rows: a retry, already reserved
UPDATE stock SET available = available - 1, reserved = reserved + 1
WHERE sku = 'SHOE-42' AND available >= 1;  -- 0 rows: sold out, ROLLBACK
COMMIT;

steps.label: 1 row updated
steps.detail: Zero rows would mean sold out. The reservation is a hold, not a sale: it becomes a sale when the order is paid, or the sweeper releases it if the checkout is abandoned before payment.

steps.label: charge, key = o_501
steps.detail: If the provider times out, retry with the same key: the provider returns the original result rather than charging twice. The call leaves through the NAT gateway with the API key from the secrets manager, and the provider's own fraud screening runs on the charge.

steps.label: commit reservation o_501
steps.detail: Turns the hold into a sale before the order is marked paid, so the sweeper can never put sold stock back on the shelf. If the service crashes here, the order is still PENDING and the sweeper finishes the job.

steps.label: UPDATE reservation COMMITTED
steps.detail: Conditional on HELD, so a retry changes nothing.

steps.label: UPDATE PAID + INSERT outbox
steps.detail: Transactional outbox: the status change and the OrderPaid event commit together. There is never a paid order without its event, or an event without the order.

steps.label: poll outbox
steps.detail: Or tail the database change log (CDC). Either way, only committed rows are published.

steps.label: publish OrderPaid
steps.detail: At least once: a crash after publishing but before marking the row sends the event again, so every consumer must tolerate duplicates, deduplicating by event id where a repeat would matter.

steps.label: send confirmation
steps.detail: An occasional duplicate confirmation after a crash is tolerated, so the worker needs no dedupe store. An event that keeps failing goes to the dead-letter topic instead of blocking its partition.

flows.title: Payment declined (saga rollback)
flows.summary: No distributed transaction: each completed step has a compensating action that undoes it.

steps.label: POST /orders
steps.detail: Same path as a successful order: WAF, CDN (not cached), gateway, internal load balancer.

steps.label: release reservation
steps.detail: Compensating action for the reservation. It is idempotent too, so a retried release cannot add stock twice.

steps.label: release reservation
steps.detail: Guarded by the reservation row: stock goes back only if this call moved it from HELD to RELEASED.

steps.label: UPDATE FAILED + outbox
steps.detail: OrderFailed is published the same way as OrderPaid.

steps.label: Card declined, try another
steps.detail: The same cart can be retried with a new idempotency key.

flows.title: Provider timeout, settled by the sweeper
flows.summary: The charge outcome is unknown, so the order stays PENDING with its stock held. The sweeper asks the provider again and finishes the order.

steps.label: charge o_503
steps.detail: Order o_503 was created and its stock reserved exactly as in the main flow.

steps.label: charge, key = o_503
steps.detail: Two attempts with the same key and a short timeout. This path is rare, so it sits outside the 2 s p99, but the shopper still gets an answer within a few seconds.

steps.label: timeout (twice)
steps.detail: A timeout is not a decline: the provider may have charged the card and the answer was lost.

steps.label: 202 Accepted, pending
steps.detail: Never fail an order whose charge might have succeeded, and never release its stock. The order stays PENDING.

steps.label: Confirming your payment…
steps.detail: The page polls GET /orders/o_503 (also uncached) until the order settles.

steps.label: every minute: sweep stuck orders
steps.detail: A background loop in every Order Service instance; no leader is needed because each claim below skips rows another instance holds. It also releases the reservations of orders older than 15 minutes whose charge never started (no payment attempt recorded).

steps.label: claim PENDING > 2 min
steps.detail: Each instance takes a one-minute lease on a batch of old PENDING orders; SKIP LOCKED and the lease keep two instances off the same order, and every later step is idempotent anyway.
steps.payload:
UPDATE orders SET sweep_lease_until = now() + interval '1 minute'
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND created_at < now() - interval '2 minutes'
    AND (sweep_lease_until IS NULL OR sweep_lease_until < now())
  ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING id;

steps.label: repeat charge, key = o_503
steps.detail: Repeating the request with the same key is the safe question: if the first attempt charged, the provider replays that result; if it never arrived, the charge happens now, which is still what the order wants. Provider idempotency keys are kept for at least a day, far longer than this window.

steps.label: succeeded (replayed)
steps.detail: Had it been declined, the order service would release the reservation and mark the order FAILED, as in the declined flow. While the provider stays unreachable the order simply stays PENDING.

steps.label: UPDATE reservation COMMITTED
steps.detail: The reservation was never expired, because the sweeper does not release stock for an order whose charge has started.

steps.label: UPDATE PAID + INSERT outbox
steps.detail: The same transaction as the main flow, so the OrderPaid event and the confirmation email follow as usual.

notes.text: Saga instead of a distributed transaction: services stay independent and available; the cost is writing a compensating action for every step and accepting brief intermediate states.
Transactional outbox fixes the dual-write problem: writing to the database and publishing an event separately can fail halfway; one transaction cannot.

On a timeout the charge state is unknown. Retry with the same idempotency key; if still unknown, answer 202 and leave the order PENDING with its stock held, and let the sweeper repeat the keyed request until the provider answers. During a provider outage a circuit breaker makes new checkouts fail fast instead of reserving stock they cannot pay for.

A single hot SKU in a flash sale concentrates writes on one row, which tops out at a few hundred to a few thousand updates a second. Split its stock into several buckets (rows) and reserve from any bucket with stock. Both databases keep every commit in more than one zone (Aurora writes its storage across three zones; Cloud SQL HA keeps a synchronous standby), so losing a zone costs a failover of about a minute but no committed order.
Kafka replicates each partition across 3 zones; with one zone down it still has a majority of replicas and keeps accepting writes.

The WAF runs at the CDN edge: managed rule sets, bot control, and rate rules on POST /orders per IP, per account and per card fingerprint, because card testing (bots trying stolen cards with small orders) is the classic attack on a checkout. Card numbers never touch our servers: the browser tokenizes the card with the provider, and only the Payment Service can read the provider API key from the secrets manager.

questions.q: The shopper double-clicks "Place order". How do you avoid two orders and two charges?
questions.a: The client sends an idempotency key with the request, and the order service stores it with the order under a unique constraint on (customer, key). A repeat with the same key returns the first order instead of creating a new one. The payment call uses the order id as the provider's idempotency key, so the card is charged once.

questions.q: Inventory is reserved but the payment is declined. How does the system undo it?
questions.a: Checkout is a saga: each step has a compensating action. When payment fails, the order service releases the reservation and marks the order failed. There is no distributed transaction, so every step and every compensation must be idempotent and safe to retry.

questions.q: Why use an outbox instead of publishing the order event directly after the database write?
questions.a: Writing to the database and publishing to the broker are two systems; a crash between them loses the event or publishes one for an order that was rolled back. The outbox row is written in the same transaction as the order, and the relay publishes it afterwards, so the event exists if and only if the order does. Consumers must tolerate duplicates.

questions.q: Two shoppers buy the last item at the same time. How do you avoid overselling?
questions.a: Reserve stock with an atomic conditional update that only decrements while stock is above zero, and check that a row changed; a CHECK constraint backs it up. Only one request wins. A reservation becomes a sale when the order is paid; a sweeper releases reservations of checkouts abandoned before payment, but never one whose charge is in flight.

questions.q: The payment provider times out. Do you retry, fail, or wait?
questions.a: The outcome is unknown, so retry with the same idempotency key, which is safe. If it is still unknown, answer 202, keep the order PENDING with its stock held, and let a sweeper repeat the keyed request until the provider answers paid or declined. Never fail or release an order whose charge might have succeeded.

questions.q: A flash sale sends 50 times the normal traffic at one product. What breaks first and what do you do?
questions.a: The single inventory row for that product becomes a hot spot. Rate limit at the WAF and gateway, hold buyers in a waiting room, and split stock into several counters (buckets) that are claimed independently. Keep browsing traffic on the CDN and caches so it does not compete with checkout.
